title: Proxy validation for legal query mix: prevalence of date-constrained questions across sources
research_question: Do web-QA situated questions and curated exam-style legal question sets yield prevalence estimates for date-constrained questions that agree with a real legal information-seeking source, or do they differ enough that neither can serve as a validated proxy?
hypothesis: Web-QA situated questions and curated exam-style legal question sets are not interchangeable proxies for the prevalence of date-constrained questions in real legal information-seeking traffic: the curated sets understate it because authority is supplied, the web-QA figure overstates it because it counts geographical as well as temporal dependence, and prevalence differs enough across sources that no single constant is defensible.
proposed_method: Sample questions from several candidate sources under fixed sampling frames: a curated legal MCQA set, situated web-QA questions, and a real information-seeking legal source such as a public legal question-and-answer archive, optionally supplemented by statutory-interpretation questions drawn from published judgments. Two annotators independently label each question using a written codebook distinguishing current-state, past-state and explicitly dated questions, plus whether the answer depends on a version that has since been superseded; disagreements are adjudicated and agreement reported. Estimate prevalence per source with confidence intervals, test pairwise differences, and compute a calibration factor between each proxy and the real-traffic estimate. Feed the resulting range into the prevalence weighting plan as a labelled assumption rather than a validated constant.
baselines: The web-QA prevalence figure (roughly 16.5% context-dependent) as the working prior being tested
Curated exam-style legal QA and MCQA sets as the second candidate proxy
The real-traffic source's own prevalence estimate as the reference standard
A null model in which prevalence is treated as heterogeneous by construction, so no single proxy can be validated
datasets: Candidate real-traffic sources: public legal question-and-answer archives with enough volume for stable estimation, and statutory-interpretation reasoning in published judgments as a second, non-asker-generated source
Candidate proxy sources already in hand: situated web QA questions and curated legal MCQA question sets
A hand-labelled sample per source with two independent annotations and adjudicated labels
Not used as prevalence sources: ESG disclosure questions and financial filing QA
workloads: Sampling under fixed frames from a public legal question-and-answer archive
Sampling from curated legal MCQA and exam-style sets
Sampling from situated web-QA questions with temporal or geographical dependence
Two-annotator labelling with adjudication across all sources
Statistical comparison and calibration against the real-traffic estimate
hardware: CPU-only: sampling and annotation of question text plus statistical estimation. No models are required beyond optional embedding-based near-duplicate detection during sampling; annotation is human.
metrics: Prevalence of date-constrained questions per source, with confidence intervals and raw counts
Three-way breakdown into current-state, past-state and explicitly dated questions per source
Inter-annotator agreement (for example Krippendorff's alpha) on the classification, and adjudication rate
Pairwise prevalence differences between sources with tests and intervals
Calibration factor between each proxy and the real-traffic estimate, with interval
Proportion of questions whose correct answer depends on a superseded version, as the quantity the benchmark actually conditions on
ablations: Source used as the real-traffic anchor: public legal Q&A, statutory-interpretation passages in judgments, practitioner-authored compliance questions, or a query log if one can be obtained
Annotation granularity: binary date-constrained vs not, versus a three-way split of current-state, past-state and explicitly dated questions
Whether dependence on a superseded version is judged by the annotator or derived from the legal text's amendment history
Sampling frame within a source: recent vs historical questions, jurisdiction, subject area
Single-annotator provisional labels vs two-annotator adjudicated labels, to quantify the cost of reduced annotation
controls: Identical codebook and annotation instructions across all sources
The same annotator pair applied across sources to prevent annotator-source confounding
Fixed sample size per source with the sampling rule recorded
Prevalence reported with confidence intervals and raw counts, never as a bare percentage
Annotation performed blind to the research hypothesis about oversampling
Every source's sampling frame, collection date and inclusion rule documented
confounders_addressed: Annotation subjectivity on what counts as date-constrained - addressed by two independent annotators, a written codebook, adjudication and a reported agreement statistic
Source composition effects such as question length, formality or whether the asker is a professional - addressed by sampling within a fixed frame and reporting source-level descriptive statistics

Selection bias in public Q&A toward unusual or contested questions - addressed by reporting the sampling frame explicitly and treating the estimate as bounding rather than exact, with the direction of likely bias argued
Low base rates producing unstable estimates - addressed by pre-registering a sample size targeting a confidence interval width around the estimate
Transfer from written questions to real spoken client queries being untestable from public data - acknowledged as a residual limitation rather than assumed away
expected_outcomes: Proxy prevalence figures do not transfer directly: the curated exam-style sets are expected to show little or no date-constrained prevalence because authority is supplied by construction, the web-QA figure is expected to overstate the legal rate because it counts geographical dependence, and the real-traffic source is expected to sit somewhere in between with a wide interval. The result is a calibration table and, at minimum, an argument for reporting prevalence as a swept variable rather than a constant. If the sources surprisingly agree, the proxy is validated and the weighted estimate can be quoted with more confidence.
failure_conditions: No real-traffic source can be sampled at a size that yields a usable confidence interval - the question remains open and only the sensitivity sweep can be reported
Proxy and real-traffic prevalences differ so much that no single calibration factor is defensible - then the weighted deployment figure must be dropped in favour of stratum-separated reporting
Inter-annotator agreement on what counts as date-constrained is too low to support any prevalence estimate
Date-constrained prevalence turns out to be near zero in the real-traffic source, which would undercut the practical significance of the whole line of work while leaving the mechanism interesting
Sampling frames differ on unmeasured dimensions that plausibly drive the difference, making any comparison uninterpretable
reproducibility_notes: No execution spec is attached: the study requires human annotation and sampling from sources that must be collected under their own terms of use, and no public implementation exists to run. To make it reproducible: pre-register the sampling frames, inclusion rules, target sample sizes and the annotation codebook; record collection dates and the exact query used to obtain each sample; publish the codebook and the adjudicated labels with de-identified question text where redistribution permits; report raw counts alongside estimates and state the direction of likely sampling bias; and make the resulting prevalence range the input to the weighting plan so downstream numbers can be recomputed if the range changes.
